short.headline: India really has the biggest jobs challenge in the developing world
short.dek: Projections show about 238 million young Indians will reach working age by 2035, more than any other developing economy.
short.body: India faces the largest absolute wave of new workers among developing economies, with about 238 million projected to reach working age by 2035, according to a new World Bank report. That is roughly one in five of the entire developing world's youth pipeline, and it surpasses the totals of many whole regions. Yet these numbers are demographic projections, not counts of the unemployed. India's youth population has already stopped growing, and whether the economy needs 60 million or 148 million new jobs by 2030 hinges largely on labour-force participation, above all whether more women enter the workforce. The headline is sobering, but the fine print restores proportion: India's challenge is one of sheer scale, not unique youthfulness, and the window is already beginning to close.

macha.heading: Okay, but what does this actually mean, macha?
macha.body: Picture this: the Indian economy needs to create space for nearly 238 million young people entering the working age over the next decade. That's more than China, more than any other country. But don't let that number scare you – it's the number of people who will be of working age, not the jobless count. And here's the twist: India's youth bulge has actually peaked already, so the pressure is at its highest right now. What decides if this becomes a crisis or a dividend is simple: if more Indian women find work, the job gap widens sharply; if not, it shrinks. So the real question is not about how many young people we have, but whether the economy and society can put them to work – especially the women.
macha.soWhat: The number is huge, but it's a choice, not a destiny.

article.title: Does India really have the biggest jobs challenge in the world?
article.standfirst: India alone accounts for about 238 million young people reaching working age over 2025-35, more than any other developing economy. But the number is a projection of supply, not a count of the unemployed, and the youth wave has already crested.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## Does India have the biggest youth workforce challenge among developing economies?

Yes. About 238 million people are projected to reach working age (15-24) in India between 2025 and 2035, the highest of any developing economy. Next is China with about 169 million, then Nigeria (61 million), Pakistan (59 million), and Indonesia (47 million). This is the 'youth method' from a new World Bank study, and it counts the young arriving, not the unemployed. India's lead comes from its enormous population, not a unique youth bulge. The countries with the highest share of young people, like the Central African Republic and Niger, are far smaller. So the size of the task is staggering, but the intensity is not.

> India alone accounts for about 238 million of them, close to one in five of the developing world's total.

## Is India's challenge comparable to that of entire regions?

Yes, India's pipeline rivals multi-country regions. The developing world as a whole has a massive youth pipeline; India's 238 million is roughly one in five of it. India alone accounts for about 86% of all South Asia (278 million) and around 72% of Sub-Saharan Africa (332 million). It surpasses the entire Middle East and North Africa (170 million), Latin America and the Caribbean (99 million), and Europe and Central Asia (65 million). So when we say India faces the biggest jobs challenge, we are comparing one country to whole regions.

## Does India still lead when we look at the whole working-age population over a longer period?

Yes. Switching to a broader measure, the net increase in people aged 15 to 64, all potential workers, not just the young, India adds about 132 million between 2025 and 2050. That is more than Nigeria (about 98 million), Pakistan (89 million), the Democratic Republic of Congo (72 million), and Ethiopia (67 million). Over the shorter 2025-35 window, the net increase is about 91 million, more than twice Nigeria's 40 million. The three methods the report uses give different absolute numbers globally, roughly 270 million, 447 million, or 1.23 billion depending on the method, but India consistently ranks first. The lead is not a statistical quirk.

## Is India's youth population still growing?

Surprisingly, no. The growth rate of India's 15-24 population has already turned negative. It peaked at 2.2% a year around 2000 and crossed below zero about 2021. Projections show it falling further to about -0.8% by 2040. This means the number of young people is no longer getting bigger. The wave of new entrants has crested. Yet the absolute number remains the largest on earth for years, so the economy must still absorb a massive cohort. Think of a high tide that has stopped rising but hasn't yet receded.

## What about the broader working-age population?

The working-age group (15-64) tells the same story, just later. Its annual growth rate peaked at 2.5% in 2000 and declines steadily, turning slightly negative around 2050 at -0.1%. That is far in the future, and the actual number of working-age people will keep expanding until then, but the engine is slowing. By mid-century, India's labour pool will stop growing. This is the closing of the demographic window, still open, but narrowing.

## How does India's overall population compare to China's?

India is now the world's most populous country, overtaking China around 2022-23. According to projections, India's population will continue rising until about 2060 before gently declining, while China's is already shrinking. In 1990, China had 1.15 billion people to India's 0.87 billion; by 2100, those numbers are projected to be 0.63 billion and 1.51 billion. Population is the ceiling for the workforce, not the workforce itself. The challenge is to turn demographic heft into productive employment, not just to count bodies.

## What determines whether the jobs gap is 60 million or 148 million?

A study from the IMF (Alonso and MacDonald 2024) cited in the World Bank report shows a stark sensitivity. If India's labour-force participation rate stays flat, the country would need about 60 million new jobs by 2030. But if participation rises toward a target rate, which largely means more women joining the workforce, the number jumps to 148 million. By 2050, the range widens from 143 million to 324 million. These scenarios are not forecasts; they illustrate an important lever. The demographic numbers set the stage, but it is participation, above all of women, that writes the script.

> Whether India needs 60 million or 148 million new jobs by 2030 hinges on one lever above all: labour-force participation, which in India means whether more women enter the workforce.

## How should you read these numbers?

This page is built almost entirely on one source: the World Bank's The Global Jobs Challenge (2026 advance edition), edited by Tommy Chrimes, M. Ayhan Kose and Kersten Stamm, using UN World Population Prospects 2024. The 60-148 million range comes from an IMF study the report cites. Every number here is a demographic projection, based on assumptions about births, deaths, and migration, not a measurement of current unemployment. The three counting methods (youth, working-age, ratio) produce very different global totals, so the ranking is more reliable than any single figure. The 'jobs challenge' counts young people reaching working age, not the unemployed. And this page deliberately does not include India's own labour-force or female participation rates because the source does not cover them. Use these numbers to grasp the scale and the direction of the task, not as precise job targets.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The population aged 15 to 24. Think of it as the group of young people who are either finishing education or just starting their working lives.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The 'youth method' of the jobs challenge counts how many people from this cohort will reach working age in the next decade. It is the headline number for India (about 238 million).

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The population aged 15 to 64. It is the broad pool of people considered old enough and young enough to work. The 15-24 group is part of it, but it also includes people in their prime working years and those nearing retirement.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The 'working-age method' captures net increases in this wider pool, showing India's challenge is not just about the young. India adds about 132 million working-age people from 2025 to 2050.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The share of the working-age population that is either employed or actively looking for work. If you think of the working-age population as all adults in a village, the participation rate tells you what fraction of them are out trying to earn a living.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Whether India needs 60 million or 148 million new jobs by 2030 depends almost entirely on how many women and men actually join the workforce. The range comes from scenarios assuming flat or rising participation.
glossaryBlocks.whyThisKeyTerm: This is the single most important lever converting a demographic projection into an actual jobs target. Without understanding participation, the reader cannot interpret the final chart.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A calculation of what a population will look like in the future, based on assumptions about births, deaths, and migration. It is not a prediction but a 'what if' scenario using stable patterns.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: All the numbers on this page are projections, not measurements. They are fairly reliable for the next decade because the people already exist, but they become more uncertain the further out they go.
glossaryBlocks.whyThisKeyTerm: The reader must constantly remember that these are projections, not counts. The entire page rests on this distinction.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Emerging Market and Developing Economies. These are countries that are not high-income advanced economies; they include India, China, Nigeria, Pakistan, and many others.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The World Bank report focuses on the jobs challenge in EMDEs. When we compare India to 'all EMDEs' or to other regions, we are comparing it within this group of developing economies.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The percentage of a country's total population that falls in the 15-24 age group. It tells you how 'young' a country is in relative terms, unlike the absolute number of young people.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India has the largest absolute number of young people, but not the highest youth share. That distinction belongs to much smaller economies. This is the scale-not-intensity rule.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The change in the number of people in a population group after accounting for both entries (people turning 15) and exits (people turning 65 or dying). It can be positive or negative.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The working-age method uses net increases to measure how many more potential workers an economy must absorb over a period, stripping out the effect of ageing out of the bracket.

chartExplainers.title: India tops the developing world's jobs challenge
chartExplainers.takeaway: India is projected to have 238 million young people reach working age over 2025-35, the highest among developing economies.
chartExplainers.detail: The bars show the projected number of people entering the 15-24 age group in the ten years from 2025 to 2035 for the top ten developing economies. India leads with 238 million, far ahead of China (169 million), Nigeria (61 million), Pakistan (59 million), and Indonesia (47 million). This is a demographic supply projection, not a count of the unemployed. The size of India's youth cohort reflects its huge population; smaller countries like the Central African Republic may have a higher youth share but not the absolute numbers. The data comes from UN World Population Prospects 2024 and is the central measure in the World Bank's Global Jobs Challenge report.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This is the single headline finding: of every developing economy, India must absorb the largest wave of new workers this decade.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A horizontal bar chart; the length of each bar is the projected number in millions. Look for India's bar at the top, extending far beyond the others.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not interpret the numbers as the current unemployed. They count people who will reach working age, whether or not they look for work.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a phone, each bar and its label are displayed in a vertical list, easy to read.

chartExplainers.title: One country, a fifth of the problem
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's 238 million young entrants rival the totals of entire developing regions, including 86% of South Asia and 72% of Sub-Saharan Africa.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart sets India's youth pipeline against the collective totals of six EMDE regions. India's 238 million is just under the 278 million of South Asia as a whole, and 72% of Sub-Saharan Africa's 332 million. It exceeds the Middle East and North Africa (170 million), Latin America and the Caribbean (99 million), and Europe and Central Asia (65 million). The comparison underscores that India's challenge is continental in scale, while other regions spread it across dozens of countries.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To feel the scale, set India alone against entire world regions rather than other single countries.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Another horizontal bar chart; observe that India (one country) sits near the top, close to multi-country regions.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The chart compares India to regions, not to individual countries. Do not conclude India has more young people than all of Sub-Saharan Africa; rather, its number is a very large fraction of that region's total.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Bars are stacked vertically; scrolling down reveals how India sits between whole regions.

chartExplainers.title: Still the biggest a generation out
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's projected net increase in working-age population (15-64) of 132 million over 2025-50 is the largest among developing economies.
chartExplainers.detail: The bars show net additions to the 15-64 age group between 2025 and 2050, after accounting for aging and mortality. India's 132 million tops the list, followed by Nigeria (98 million), Pakistan (89 million), the Democratic Republic of Congo (72 million), and Ethiopia (67 million). This measure captures the total growth in potential workers, not just young entrants. Even with an older population, India remains the largest contributor. The different counting methods produce varying totals, but the ranking is consistent.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The headline is not an artefact of one counting method: switch to net working-age growth and stretch to 2050, India still leads.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars show net change in millions from 2025 to 2050. Compare the length of India's bar to the next ones.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These numbers are much larger than the youth method; that's because they cover a broader age range and a longer period. Don't mix up the two measures.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A simple bar list, easy to scan.

chartExplainers.title: The wave has already crested
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's 15-24 population growth rate has fallen from 2.2% in 2000 to a projected -0.8% in 2040, indicating the youth surge has passed its peak.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart traces the annual percentage growth of India's youth population from 2000 to 2040. The rate was 2.2% at the start, reflecting rapid expansion. It steadily declines, crossing below zero around 2021, and is projected to reach -0.8% by 2040. Negative growth means the total number of young people is no longer increasing; the absolute size remains very large, but the wave has stopped building. This is a crucial turning point: the demographic pressure is most intense right now.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The twist behind the big number: India's youth cohort is no longer growing, even as it stays the largest on earth.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Notice where the line crosses the horizontal zero line (around 2021) and how it continues downward.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Negative growth does not mean few young people; it means the group is not getting larger. The absolute count is still enormous.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A single line chart with clear y-axis labels; pinch to zoom if needed.

chartExplainers.title: Even the working-age pool is flattening
chartExplainers.takeaway: Growth in India's 15-64 population is projected to slow from 2.5% in 2000 to -0.1% in 2050, signalling the end of the 'demographic dividend' era.
chartExplainers.detail: A companion line chart for the wider working-age group. The annual growth rate peaked at 2.5% in 2000 and has been falling ever since. It remains positive until around 2050, when it turns slightly negative. This lag reflects the time it takes for the youth slowdown to feed into the broader pool. While the absolute number of working-age people will still grow for a few decades, the rate of increase is shrinking, meaning the window of abundant labour is gradually closing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It is not just the youngest cohort: the whole 15-64 pool, the people an economy actually puts to work, is on the same downward path, a beat behind.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the line's gentle decline toward zero; the small negative value at the end shows the pool beginning to shrink.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The pool is still adding tens of millions of people in absolute terms during the 2030s and 2040s, even as the growth rate falls. The chart shows deceleration, not an immediate loss of workers.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Simple line chart; the trend is clear even at a glance.

chartExplainers.title: The largest workforce on earth, but cresting
chartExplainers.takeaway: India overtook China in total population around 2022 and will remain the most populous country this century, but its own population growth is slowing.
chartExplainers.detail: Two lines show total population projections from 1990 to 2100. India's line crosses China's around 2022, then continues rising, peaking around 2060 before a gentle decline. China's line, after peaking earlier, falls steadily. In 1990, China had 1.15 billion and India 0.87 billion; by 2100, the projections are 0.63 billion and 1.51 billion. This divergence sets the stage for India's long-term workforce potential, but population alone does not guarantee jobs; participation and economic structure are decisive.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Context for the workforce story: India overtook China to become the world's most populous economy, but its own population peaks within a generation.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Follow the two lines: India's upward then flattening, China's downward. The crossing point is the overtake.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Population size provides a ceiling, not a direct count of workers. A large population can mean either a demographic dividend or a burden depending on job creation.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Dual line chart; colour coding distinguishes the countries. Use large labels for accessibility.

chartExplainers.title: A 60-million job problem, or a 148-million one
chartExplainers.takeaway: Jobs needed by 2030 range from 60 million (if participation stays flat) to 148 million (if it rises), illustrating the decisive role of labour-force participation.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart presents four bars from an IMF study: two scenarios for 2030 and two for 2050. Under flat participation, India would need 60 million new jobs by 2030 and 143 million by 2050. Under a scenario of rising participation toward a target rate, the numbers jump to 148 million and 324 million. The difference within each year is driven by assumptions about how many working-age Indians—especially women—join the labour force. These are not forecasts but illustrations of sensitivity.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How big the task actually is comes down to one variable the report keeps returning to: whether Indians, above all women, join the workforce.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the two bars for each year: the short bar is flat participation, the long bar is rising participation. The gap between them shows the leverage of participation.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are conditional scenarios, not predictions. They show what would happen if certain assumptions hold; actual outcomes depend on policy and social change.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Grouped bars work well on a phone; label each bar clearly.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: Yes, India faces the largest absolute jobs task among developing economies, with about 238 million young people projected to reach working age over 2025-35, roughly one in five of the developing world's total, though the challenge is one of scale not intensity, the youth wave has already crested, and the final number of jobs needed hinges on labour-force participation especially of women.
requiredConcepts: The source discipline: almost every number comes from the World Bank's 'The Global Jobs Challenge' (2026 advance edition), using UN World Population Prospects 2024. The 60–148 million range is from an IMF study cited in the report, not the World Bank's own count.

The headline: by the 'youth method', India must absorb about 238 million young people reaching working age over 2025–35, the largest of any developing economy, ahead of China (about 169 million), Nigeria (about 61 million), Pakistan (about 59 million), and Indonesia (about 47 million). This counts people reaching working age, not the unemployed.

The scale frame: across all emerging and developing economies the youth-method total is about 1.23 billion, so India's roughly 238 million is close to one in five. Set India alone against whole regions: it is about 86% of all South Asia (about 278 million), around 72% of all Sub-Saharan Africa (about 332 million), and larger on its own than the Middle East and North Africa, Latin America, or Europe and Central Asia regions.

Robustness (working-age method): India is first not only by the youth count. By net increase in working-age population (15–64) it adds about 91 million over 2025–35 (more than twice Nigeria's roughly 40 million) and about 132 million over 2025–50 (ahead of Nigeria's roughly 98 million and Pakistan's roughly 89 million).

The method caveat: the report's three methods (youth, working-age, ratio) give very different totals. The all-EMDE jobs challenge ranges from about 270 million (ratio) to about 447 million (working-age) to about 1.23 billion (youth). Use the methods as a consistent ranking, not as precise counts.

The twist: India's youth cohort has already stopped growing. The annual growth rate of the 15–24 population crossed below zero around 2021 and stays negative thereafter. The absolute number reaching working age is still the largest on earth, but the wave has crested.

The population context: India overtook China to become the world's most populous country around 2022–23 and its population rises to a peak near 1.70 billion around 2061 before slowly declining, while China is already in sustained decline.

The participation lever: how many jobs India actually needs depends overwhelmingly on labour-force participation, above all women's. Holding participation at today's rate implies about 60 million new jobs by 2030; lifting it toward a target rate implies about 148 million. By 2050 the span is roughly 143 to 324 million. This is from the IMF study cited in the report.

The scale-not-intensity rule: India ranks first in absolute numbers on a working-age base of about one billion. It is not the most youth-dense economy; the highest youth shares are in much smaller economies like the Central African Republic, Niger, and several Pacific islands. India's challenge is sheer volume, not an unusually young population.

What this page deliberately does not claim: the report does not contain India's own employment, unemployment, or female labour-force participation levels, nor sectoral, state, or informality breakdowns. This page describes the size of the task ahead, not the current state of India's labour market.

The policy note: the report points to labour-intensive, export-oriented sectors and to services, including high-skilled services, as ways to create jobs at scale, and notes India's early-1990s trade liberalisation preceded an investment acceleration. These are suggestions, not proven fixes.

Number discipline: every statistic comes from the evidence packet; never invent or recall. Present numbers as rounded approximations (about 238 million, roughly one in five, around 132 million). These are projections, so prefer 'projected to' and 'on these estimates' over flat statements of fact.

The macha layer should be warm and grounded: yes, India has the largest jobs challenge on earth, but the number is a projection not a prophecy, it measures young people arriving not people jobless, India is the biggest because it is huge rather than because it is the youngest, the wave has already crested, and whether the task is 60 million or 148 million depends most on whether India's women get the chance to work.

sectionPlan.caveat: Negative growth means the number has peaked, but the absolute level remains enormous. The 'window' is not closed, just closing.

sectionPlan.heading: What about the broader working-age population?
sectionPlan.job: Broaden the cresting story to the entire 15–64 pool. Show the second line chart: growth in the working-age population is also falling, from 2.5% in 2000 to about –0.1% by 2050. Explain that this pool continues to grow in absolute terms for longer than the youth cohort, but the deceleration is the same pattern.
lockedNumbersToUse: Even the working-age pool is starting to flatten, latest (-0.1%)
Even the working-age pool is starting to flatten, earliest (2.5%)
conceptsToExplain: working-age population (15–64) as the pool of potential workers
the lag between youth cresting and working-age cresting
sectionPlan.caveat: The working-age pool continues to expand in absolute terms until mid-century, even as the growth rate declines.

sectionPlan.heading: How does India's overall population compare to China's?
sectionPlan.job: Provide population context. India overtook China around 2022–23 to become the world's most populous country, and its population rises to a peak near 1.70 billion around 2061, while China's declines. Use this to explain the immense potential workforce ceiling, but stress that population is not the workforce; participation and job creation determine outcomes.
lockedNumbersToUse: India, total population, latest (1.51 billion)
India, total population, earliest (0.87 billion)
China, total population, latest (0.63 billion)
China, total population, earliest (1.15 billion)
conceptsToExplain: population vs workforce (population sets the ceiling, participation sets the floor)
sectionPlan.caveat: Population projections to 2100 are uncertain. The overtake is recent history, but the peak is three decades away.

sectionPlan.heading: What determines whether the jobs gap is 60 million or 148 million?
sectionPlan.job: Introduce the participation sensitivity from the IMF study. Show the two scenarios for 2030 and 2050: holding participation flat yields about 60 million (2030) and 143 million (2050); raising participation to a target yields 148 million (2030) and 324 million (2050). Explain that this lever, above all female labour-force participation, is what converts a demographic projection into a jobs target. Label it clearly as an IMF-cited figure.

A 60-million job problem, or a 148-million one: value (148)

A 60-million job problem, or a 148-million one: value (324)
conceptsToExplain: why women's participation determines the range
sectionPlan.caveat: These numbers come from an IMF study cited in the report, not from the World Bank directly. They illustrate sensitivity, not policy targets.

sectionPlan.heading: How should you read these numbers?
sectionPlan.job: A short, honest methodology close. Name the source: the World Bank's 'The Global Jobs Challenge' (2026 advance edition, edited by Tommy Chrimes, M. Ayhan Kose and Kersten Stamm), with population data from the UN World Population Prospects 2024, and the 60–148 range from the IMF study (Alonso and MacDonald 2024). State that these are demographic projections, not measurements; the three methods give very different estimates so the ranking is more reliable; the 'jobs challenge' counts people reaching working age, not the unemployed; and this page does not contain India's own labour-force or female-participation levels because the report does not include them.
conceptsToExplain: what the three methods count differently
sectionPlan.caveat: None beyond the whole-page caveats already stated.

chartPlan.title: India tops the developing world's jobs challenge
chartPlan.whyShowThis: This is the single headline finding: of every developing economy, India must absorb the largest wave of new workers this decade.
chartPlan.howToRead: It is a horizontal bar chart; the length of each bar shows the projected number of young people reaching working age between 2025 and 2035, in millions. Look for India's bar at the top, which extends far beyond the others.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Do not interpret the numbers as the current unemployed. They are demographic projections of supply, not a headcount of people without work.

chartPlan.title: One country, a fifth of the problem
chartPlan.whyShowThis: To feel the scale, set India alone against entire world regions rather than other single countries.
chartPlan.howToRead: Another horizontal bar chart comparing India to EMDE regions. Observe that India's number is close to four-fifths of South Asia's total and surpasses several whole regions.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: The regions are groups of many countries; India is a single country. Do not conclude that India has a larger challenge than Sub-Saharan Africa, only that it rivals the region in absolute size.

chartPlan.title: Still the biggest a generation out
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The headline is not an artefact of one counting method: switch to net working-age growth and stretch to 2050, India still leads.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bars show the net increase in population aged 15–64 from 2025 to 2050. India's bar is at the top again.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: The absolute numbers here are very different from the youth-method chart; that is expected because the methods count different things. Focus on the ranking, not the precise magnitude.

chartPlan.title: The wave has already crested
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The twist behind the big number: India's youth cohort is no longer growing, even as it stays the largest on earth.
chartPlan.howToRead: A line chart tracking the annual percentage growth of the 15–24 population over time. Look for the point where the line crosses below zero, indicating the number of young people has stopped increasing.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A negative growth rate does not mean there are suddenly few young people; it means the group is no longer getting bigger. The absolute number remains massive.

chartPlan.title: Even the working-age pool is flattening
chartPlan.whyShowThis: It is not just the youngest cohort: the whole 15–64 pool, the people an economy actually puts to work, is on the same downward path.
chartPlan.howToRead: A similar line chart for the growth rate of the 15–64 population. Note that the growth stays positive for longer than the youth chart, but the downward trend is unmistakable.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Flattening growth still means the pool is adding millions each year in absolute terms until mid-century. The chart shows deceleration, not decline in the number of working-age people.

chartPlan.title: The largest workforce on earth, but cresting
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Context for the workforce story: India overtook China to become the world's most populous economy, but its own population peaks within a generation.
chartPlan.howToRead: A dual line chart with India and China's total population from 1990 to 2100. See where the Indian line crosses the Chinese line and how India's line eventually levels off, while China's falls.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Population is not the same as workforce. A large population gives a large potential labour pool, but only if people participate.

chartPlan.title: A 60-million job problem, or a 148-million one
chartPlan.whyShowThis: How big the task actually is comes down to one variable the report keeps returning to: whether Indians, above all women, join the workforce.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bars compare two scenarios for each time horizon (2030 and 2050): one assuming flat labour-force participation, one assuming a rise to a target rate. The gap between the two bars for each year shows the enormous sensitivity.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These scenarios do not predict what will happen; they show what would happen under different assumptions about participation. The actual number will depend on policy and social change.

visualizationDecisions.reason: Ranking data with a few large categories; horizontal bars are easy to read on a small phone screen.
Same reasoning, comparing one country to regions.
Consistent with other ranking charts; a longer window shown in one bar.
Trend of a growth rate over time; a line shows the direction and pace of decline clearly.
Similar trend, slightly longer window; line ensures comparability with youth growth chart.
Direct comparison of two population trajectories over a century; two lines are cleaner than bars.
Scenario comparisons; side-by-side bars for each year make the sensitivity easy to see.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The population aged 15 to 24. Think of it as the group of young people who are either finishing education or just starting their working lives.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The 'youth method' of the jobs challenge counts how many people from this cohort will reach working age in the next decade. It is the headline number for India (about 238 million).

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The population aged 15 to 64. It is the broad pool of people considered old enough and young enough to work. The 15–24 group is part of it, but it also includes people in their prime working years and those nearing retirement.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The 'working-age method' captures net increases in this wider pool, showing India's challenge is not just about the young. India adds about 132 million working-age people from 2025 to 2050.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The share of the working-age population that is either employed or actively looking for work. If you think of the working-age population as all adults in a village, the participation rate tells you what fraction of them are out trying to earn a living.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Whether India needs 60 million or 148 million new jobs by 2030 depends almost entirely on how many women and men actually join the workforce. The range comes from scenarios assuming flat or rising participation.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A calculation of what a population will look like in the future, based on assumptions about births, deaths, and migration. It is not a prediction but a 'what if' scenario using stable patterns.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: All the numbers on this page are projections, not measurements. They are fairly reliable for the next decade because the people already exist, but they become more uncertain the further out they go.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Emerging Market and Developing Economies. These are countries that are not high-income advanced economies; they include India, China, Nigeria, Pakistan, and many others.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The World Bank report focuses on the jobs challenge in EMDEs. When we compare India to 'all EMDEs' or to other regions, we are comparing it within this group of developing economies.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The percentage of a country's total population that falls in the 15–24 age group. It tells you how 'young' a country is in relative terms, unlike the absolute number of young people.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India has the largest absolute number of young people, but not the highest youth share. That distinction belongs to much smaller economies. This is the scale-not-intensity rule.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The change in the number of people in a population group after accounting for both entries (people turning 15) and exits (people turning 65 or dying). It can be positive or negative.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The working-age method uses net increases to measure how many more potential workers an economy must absorb over a period, stripping out the effect of ageing out of the bracket.

Number discipline: every statistic must come from the locked numbers in the evidence packet

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
